title: the Vishnu Purana (selections)
tomorrow: a king gives up everything for one promise. right or wrong?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vishnu Purana and Kandu, whose one evening lasted centuries because he stopped counting. Today the book counts time on a far bigger scale: whole ages of the world.

Every so often a post goes around saying this generation is the worst one yet. Shorter attention, softer, more lost. The Vishnu Purana knows that mood. Its last book describes the Kali age, the hardest of the world's ages, the one tradition says we live in now. And then, a strange scene. Sages come to Vyasa with a question while he's bathing in the Ganga. He dips under, comes up, and says: Kali is excellent. He dips again and praises the Shudras. A third time, and he praises women. Then he climbs out, and the sages just stare.
screen: `THE WORST GENERATION YET?` → `VYASA IN THE GANGA.` → `THREE DIVES, THREE PRAISES.`

segments.voice: Here's the question they'd brought. When does a little effort bring the greatest reward, and who gains it most easily? Vyasa answers with the ages. What people reached in the first age by long meditation, in the second by great sacrifices, and in the third by careful worship, they reach in the Kali age by singing the name of Keshava, a name of Vishnu. The Sanskrit line ends kalau sankirtya keshavam: in Kali, by singing Keshava. So the age that looks worst is the age where the door is lowest. A practice that once took a lifetime now takes a song. That's the puzzle solved, at least the first dive. The other two are harder to hear. Vyasa praises Shudras and women because, in the order of his day, they were spared the heavy rites others had to keep, and could reach the same goal through faithful service. Some readers today find those reasons hard, and say so. Others hold on to the turn itself: a great sage, coming up out of the river, praising first the time and the people everyone else looked down on. Both reactions belong to people reading this book now.
screen: `A LITTLE EFFORT, A GREAT REWARD?` · `MEDITATION, SACRIFICE, WORSHIP.` · `IN KALI: SINGING KESHAVA'S NAME.` · `THE HARDER DIVES.` · then, large: `THE HARD AGE HAS THE LOW DOOR.`

segments.voice: Say one name slowly, out loud or just under your breath: a name of God if you pray, or the name of someone you love if you don't. Let each time land before the next one comes. When it feels finished, rest in the quiet the name leaves behind.
The Vishnu Purana. Today's piece: Vyasa in the river, calling the hardest age excellent, because in it a sung name is enough.
Keep this line: the Vishnu Purana, selections, where the hard age has the low door. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus sing or chant the names of God, alone or together in kirtan and bhajan; some teachers cite the Vishnu Purana's line on the Kali age as the reason the sung name matters so much now.

original.note: Sanskrit: the name of the last, hardest age of the world; a different word from the goddess Kālī (काली).

trapdoor: what you thought: Kali yuga is just a doom word for how bad things are now.
what it means: in the Vishnu Purana, Vyasa calls the Kali age excellent, because in it a sung name is enough.
what a scholar hears: Vishnu Purana 6.2 sets meditation, sacrifice and worship in the earlier ages beside sankirtana in Kali; kali the age and Kālī the goddess are different words.
recall: the hard age where a name is enough

chat.meaning: In Vishnu Purana 6.2, Vyasa praises the Kali age: what earlier ages reached by meditation, sacrifice and worship, it reaches by singing Keshava's name.

Vyasa.meaning: the great sage tradition credits with arranging the Vedas and Puranas

Ganga.meaning: the river Ganges, holy in Hindu tradition

Keshava.meaning: a name of Vishnu, also used for Krishna

Shudras.meaning: the laboring class in the old fourfold social order

Kali.meaning: the last and hardest of the world's four ages

notes: 2026-10-14 recipe v3 (puzzle shape: why would a sage call the worst age the best?). Written fresh; 1507–1512 not on disk when written.

Vishnu Purana 6.2: Vyasa rises from the Ganga three times saying 'Kali is excellent', 'well done, Shudra', 'women are blessed', then explains; confirm the order and the sages' question ('when does a little merit give great reward, and who performs it easily').
6.2.17, kalau sankirtya keshavam, quoted in transliteration; confirm reading and verse number. Some editions read 'tad apnoti kalau samkirtya keshavam'.

The reasons for Shudras and women (service to the twice-born; service to husbands, without the heavy rites) are summarized as 'spared the heavy rites ... faithful service'; a Keeper should check that this is fair to the text and to readers who find it hard.
'The one tradition says we live in now': hedged; confirm phrasing.
Myth/original: kali (the age, from the losing throw of the dice) and Kālī (the goddess) are different words; confirm.
Practice kind: say it out loud (a name). Priya: an aunty at garba mutters 'kali yug' at her phone.
